title: State v. Pagliai
description: Whether parties in a criminal case can, by plea agreement, confer on the district court the authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, with the State arguing such agreements are permissible based on precedent, and the defendant arguing the court lacks statutory authority for such assessments.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that its precedents (State v. Petrie and State v. McMurry) allow parties to bargain for the assessment of costs in dismissed cases, and that Pagliai waived any challenge by entering the plea agreement.
defendant_argument: Pagliai argued that the district court lacked statutory authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, making the dispositional orders invalid, and that such an unauthorized disposition cannot be cured by contract, waiver, or estoppel.
decision_outcome: The court conditionally vacated the convictions, sentences, and dispositional orders, and remanded the case, allowing the State to either vacate only the cost assessment or vacate the entire plea bargain and reinstate all charges.

title: State Public Defender v. Iowa District Court for Scott County
description: Whether a district court has a role in determining if a local public defender is experiencing a temporary overload of cases, thereby allowing it to return cases to the court.
plaintiff_argument: The local public defender has sole authority to determine if it has a temporary overload and can return cases to the court, which the court must accept.
defendant_argument: The district court has a role in determining if a temporary overload exists before a local public defender can return cases, especially when no other attorneys are available.
decision_outcome: The court sustained the State Public Defender's writ of certiorari, vacating the district court's orders and ruling that the district court exceeded its limited role by requiring an evidentiary hearing on the public defender's workload.

title: State v. Hidlebaugh
description: Whether sentencing a defendant to prison based on their financial inability to fulfill a plea agreement's condition (purchasing a home) despite good faith efforts violates constitutional rights to equal protection and due process.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court's sentence was proper, the plea agreement should be enforced, and considering Hidlebaugh's financial circumstances was a permissible sentencing factor.
defendant_argument: Hidlebaugh argued that his prison sentence was unconstitutional because it was imposed due to his financial inability to purchase a home, despite his best efforts, violating his Fourteenth Amendment rights to equal protection and due process.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals decision, vacated Hidlebaugh's sentence, and remanded the case for resentencing, ruling that sentencing based on financial inability despite good faith efforts is unconstitutional.

title: State v. Woods
description: Whether there is a federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while simultaneously in the illegal possession of a controlled substance or while committing an indictable offense.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Iowa argued that there is no federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime, specifically while illegally possessing a controlled substance or committing an indictable offense.
defendant_argument: Kevin Dwayne Woods, Jr. argued that his conviction for carrying a dangerous weapon while illegally possessing a controlled substance violates his federal and state constitutional right to keep and bear arms.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Kevin Woods's conviction for violating Iowa Code section 724.8B, ruling that there is no constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime.

title: State v. Scullark
description: Whether the search of a defendant's fanny pack, which he attempted to pass to another person before being handcuffed, violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures under the United States and Iowa Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The search was a valid search incident to arrest because the fanny pack was immediately associated with Scullark's person at the time of arrest, making it subject to a categorical rule allowing full searches without additional justification.
defendant_argument: The search violated his constitutional rights because he was unable to access the fanny pack when it was searched, and the search did not serve the purposes of officer safety or evidence preservation, thus the "reaching-distance" rule should apply.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals decision and affirmed the district court order denying Scullark's motion to suppress, thereby upholding the search of the fanny pack.

title: State v. Cole
description: Whether the firearm prohibition under Iowa Code section 724.26(2)(a) for individuals subject to a domestic violence protective order violates the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution and article I, section 1A of the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (State of Iowa) argued that Jordan Kevin Cole waived his Second Amendment and article I, section 1A rights by consenting to the protective order that prohibited him from possessing firearms.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Jordan Kevin Cole) argued that the firearm prohibition was unconstitutional under the Second Amendment and article I, section 1A of the Iowa Constitution, and that his sentencing order was unlawful.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Jordan Kevin Cole's convictions for possession of firearms while under a domestic violence protective order, but remanded the case for entry of a corrected sentencing order regarding consecutive prison sentences upon probation revocation.

title: Sikora v. Iowa
description: Whether sovereign immunity bars a former prisoner's state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment by state officials.
plaintiff_argument: Eugene Sikora claims he was wrongfully imprisoned for nearly five months due to a miscalculation of his release date and seeks money damages, arguing that sovereign immunity should not bar his constitutional tort claims or common law claims against individual state employees.
defendant_argument: The State of Iowa and its Department of Corrections director argue that sovereign immunity generally precludes state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment, and no exception applies, especially after the Burnett decision overruled Godfrey.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Eugene Sikora's tort damages suit for wrongful imprisonment, ruling that sovereign immunity bars such claims against the state and its employees.

title: State v. Amble
description: Whether police officers need a warrant to search garbage bags placed curbside for collection, with the State arguing no based on a new statute defining such garbage as abandoned property, and the defendants arguing yes based on constitutional privacy rights and prior precedent.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that Iowa Code section 808.16 is constitutional and that its provision deeming curbside garbage as abandoned property eliminates any reasonable expectation of privacy, thus allowing warrantless searches.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that Iowa Code section 808.16 is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers by attempting to redefine constitutional rights, and that they maintain a reasonable expectation of privacy in their trash.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's ruling, finding that Iowa Code section 808.16(3) is constitutional and lawfully authorized the warrantless trash pulls, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Rivas v. Brownell
description: Whether the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the plaintiff arguing it did and the defendants arguing it did not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the pandemic and that the district court erred in ruling otherwise.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the lawsuit was time-barred because the supreme court lacked the power to toll the statute of limitations, violating separation of powers and due process rights.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the supreme court's tolling provision was valid and the plaintiff's lawsuit was timely filed.

title: League of United Latin American Citizens of Iowa v. Pate
description: Whether the League of United Latin American Citizens of Iowa (LULAC) has standing to challenge a thirteen-year-old permanent injunction and seek an interpretation of the Iowa English Language Reaffirmation Act regarding non-English voting materials.
plaintiff_argument: LULAC argued it had organizational standing because the King injunction and the Secretary's interpretation of the Act impaired its voter mobilization efforts, diverted resources, and caused monetary costs, and that the Act's "rights exception" allowed non-English voting materials.
defendant_argument: The Secretary argued LULAC lacked standing because its alleged injuries were not legally cognizable and it was not a regulated party, and that the Act required all voting materials to be in English without the "rights exception" applying.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court reversed the district court's ruling, concluding that LULAC lacked standing to bring the suit, and remanded the case for dismissal.

title: State v. Mumford
description: Whether a drug detection dog's momentary intrusion into a vehicle's open window during a lawful traffic stop constitutes an unconstitutional search under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and whether there was sufficient evidence to support a conviction for possession of marijuana.
plaintiff_argument: Mumford argued that the traffic stop and the drug dog's sniff, particularly its brief intrusion into the vehicle's cabin, violated her constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures, and that there was insufficient evidence to prove the substance was marijuana.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the traffic stop was lawful, the drug dog's sniff (even with a de minimis intrusion) did not violate constitutional rights, and there was sufficient circumstantial evidence to support the conviction for possession of marijuana.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Iowa affirmed Mumford's convictions, upholding the denial of her motion to suppress evidence and finding sufficient evidence for possession of marijuana.

title: In re N.S.
description: Whether Iowa's statutory procedure for the restoration of firearm rights, lost due to an involuntary mental health commitment, survives a strict-scrutiny constitutional challenge under Amendment 1A.
plaintiff_argument: N.S. argued that Amendment 1A requires the burden of proof to shift to the State and that the current statute is unconstitutionally overbroad, thus his firearm rights should be restored.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Amendment 1A does not retroactively apply to N.S.'s 2006 commitment and that section 724.31 survives strict scrutiny as it serves a compelling interest in public safety and is narrowly tailored.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment denying N.S.'s petition for restoration of his firearm rights.

title: State v. Miller
description: Whether the sentencing of a juvenile offender to a minimum term of incarceration before parole eligibility violates the Iowa Constitution, and whether expert testimony is constitutionally required for such a sentence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that minimum terms for juvenile offenders are constitutional, expert testimony is not required for sentencing, and the district court properly exercised its sentencing discretion.
defendant_argument: Miller argued that minimum terms for juvenile offenders are unconstitutional, or if allowed, require expert testimony from the State, and that the district court abused its discretion by presuming a minimum term and misapplying factors.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed the district court's sentence of life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after serving thirty-five years, rejecting Miller's constitutional and abuse of discretion claims.

title: State v. Bauler
description: Whether a K-9 handler and trained canine momentarily making contact with the exterior of a vehicle during an open-air dog sniff constitutes an unconstitutional search under the Fourth Amendment or the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the open-air dog sniff, where the K-9 and handler physically touched the vehicle, constituted an unconstitutional search without a warrant under both the Fourth Amendment and the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that momentary contact by a K-9 during an open-air sniff does not constitute an unconstitutional search, as dog sniffs are "sui generis" and only reveal contraband, and existing precedent like Caballes controls.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's denial of the motion to suppress and affirmed the defendant's convictions and sentence.

title: State v. White
description: Whether the use of a one-way closed-circuit television system for child witness testimony, where the defendant could see the witnesses but the witnesses could not see the defendant, violated the defendant's right to face-to-face confrontation under the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the one-way video testimony procedure for child witnesses was permissible under Iowa Code and did not violate the defendant's constitutional confrontation rights, citing necessity to protect minors and existing precedent.
defendant_argument: White argued that the Iowa Constitution's confrontation clause requires face-to-face testimony with two-way visibility, and the one-way video system violated this right.
decision_outcome: The court reversed White's convictions and remanded for a new trial, holding that the one-way video testimony violated his confrontation rights under the Iowa Constitution.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc, et al. v. Kim Reynolds, et al.
description: Whether a law prohibiting abortion after a fetal heartbeat is detected is constitutional under the Iowa Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing it violates due process and other rights, and defendants arguing it is constitutional under a rational basis review.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued the fetal heartbeat statute violates the due process, inalienable rights, and equal protection clauses of the Iowa Constitution, and should be reviewed under an "undue burden" test.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued the district court applied the wrong constitutional test, and the abortion restriction should be reviewed under the less demanding "rational basis" test.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's temporary injunction, allowing the fetal heartbeat statute to take effect, finding it constitutional under the rational basis test.

title: Smith v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
description: Whether the Iowa Constitution supports a legislative privilege that protects legislators from compelled document production related to legislation, and if so, whether that privilege is absolute or qualified and applies to communications with third parties.
plaintiff_argument: The nonparty legislators argued that the Iowa Constitution provides an absolute legislative privilege protecting them from compelled document production, even for communications with third parties, and that their intent is irrelevant to LULAC's claims.
defendant_argument: LULAC argued that if a legislative privilege exists under Iowa law, it is qualified and should be abrogated in this case due to compelling constitutional rights at stake, and that discovery into individual legislators' intent is highly relevant to their First Amendment claim.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's judgment granting LULAC's motion to compel and remanded with instructions to quash the subpoenas, thereby ruling in favor of the nonparty legislators.

title: Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association v. State University of Iowa
description: Whether state universities are required members of the Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association (IIHBRA) and subject to its assessments, whether the statutory assessment scheme violates Article VII, Section 1 of the Iowa Constitution, and whether IIHBRA is entitled to late payment fees and attorney fees.
plaintiff_argument: IIHBRA argued that the universities are statutorily required members, the assessment scheme is constitutional, and it is authorized to impose late payment fees and recover attorney fees.
defendant_argument: The universities argued they are not IIHBRA members, the statutory scheme violates the Iowa Constitution by making the state a surety, and IIHBRA lacks authority to assess late payment fees or attorney fees.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the universities are IIHBRA members and the statutory scheme is constitutional, reversed the denial of late payment fees, and affirmed the denial of attorney fees, remanding for judgment including late payment fees.

title: Livingood v. City of Des Moines
description: Whether the City of Des Moines' use of the state's income offset program to collect automated traffic citation penalties not reduced to a judgment is lawful, with plaintiffs arguing it is unlawful and unconstitutional, and the city arguing it is authorized by statute.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contended the city's use of the income offset program was an unlawful property tax, violated the statute of limitations, amounted to an unconstitutional taking, was preempted by state law, violated their state constitutional right to due process of law, and constituted unjust enrichment.
defendant_argument: The city contended its use of the income offset program to collect ATE penalties was an alternative means of involuntary enforcement explicitly authorized by statute, and that the penalties fell within the meaning of "any liability" or "other qualifying debt" and its conduct was entirely lawful.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, dismissing plaintiffs' claims regarding statute of limitations, unconstitutional taking, and procedural due process, but reversing the dismissal of Livingood's preemption claim for declaratory and injunctive relief and reversing the summary judgment for the city regarding Maury and Robbins' unjust enrichment claim, remanding for further proceedings.

title: Valdez v. West Des Moines Community Schools
description: Whether the district court erred in overruling a Batson challenge to a peremptory strike and in granting a directed verdict on individual liability for constructive discharge.
plaintiff_argument: Valdez argued that the district court should have granted her Batson challenge to the peremptory strike of the only Black potential juror, that Johnson could be held individually liable for constructive discharge under the ICRA and common law, and that the district court made errors in evidentiary rulings.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that the district court properly overruled the Batson challenge based on race-neutral reasons, that Johnson was not individually liable as she was not a supervisor, and that the evidentiary rulings were correct.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the district court, ruling against Valdez on all appealed points.

title: Planned Parenthood of Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether the permanent injunction against the enforcement of Iowa Code chapter 146C's "fetal heartbeat" provision should be dissolved, thereby allowing the statute to take effect, with the plaintiff arguing against dissolution and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the injunction should remain in place because the fetal heartbeat bill is unconstitutional under the undue burden standard, which remains the governing law in Iowa, and that the statute was declared unconstitutional and not appealed, making the judgment final.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the injunction should be dissolved because there had been a substantial change in law, rendering the fetal heartbeat bill constitutional under a rational basis review, and that the district court erred in not dissolving the injunction.
decision_outcome: The court was evenly divided (3-3), resulting in the district court's ruling (denying the State's motion to dissolve the permanent injunction) being affirmed by operation of law.

title: State ex rel. Attorney General of Iowa v. Autor
description: Whether the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act's requirement that civil enforcement actions be conducted by equitable proceedings violates the constitutional right to a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that the CFA's civil actions are inherently equitable, focusing on injunctive relief and discretionary monetary remedies, thus not requiring a jury trial under the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the CFA's requirement for equitable proceedings is unconstitutional because the Attorney General was seeking substantial monetary remedies, which are legal in nature and thus entitle them to a jury trial.
decision_outcome: The district court's decision to strike the defendants' jury demand was affirmed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings.

title: Burnett v. Smith
description: Whether the Iowa Supreme Court should continue to recognize a standalone cause of action for money damages under the Iowa Constitution for alleged constitutional violations, specifically whether the precedent set in Godfrey v. State should be overruled, with the plaintiff arguing for the continued recognition of such claims and the defendant arguing for their abolishment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Cory Burnett, argued that his passive noncooperation during a vehicle inspection did not provide probable cause for his arrest for interference with official acts, and that his constitutional tort claim for damages under Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution should be endorsed, consistent with the precedent of Godfrey v. State.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Phillip Smith and the State of Iowa, argued that Godfrey v. State was wrongly decided and should be overruled, contending that the district court's grant of summary judgment in their favor was correct because there is no direct constitutional tort claim for damages without legislative authorization.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, overruling Godfrey v. State and concluding that a standalone cause of action for money damages under the Iowa Constitution is no longer recognized unless authorized by common law, an Iowa statute, or the express terms of a constitutional provision.

title: State v. Abu Youm
description: Whether the warrantless entry into Abu Youm's apartment was justified under the emergency aid doctrine, an exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement, or if it violated his constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless entry was lawful under the emergency aid doctrine because officers had an objectively reasonable belief that a serious, dangerous event was occurring, based on reports of shots fired, a man seen lying on a balcony, a broken car window, and suspicious occupant behavior.
defendant_argument: Abu Youm argued that the warrantless entry violated his Fourth Amendment rights and the Iowa Constitution, contending that no true emergency existed and the officers' actions indicated an investigatory, not caretaking, purpose, thus requiring suppression of all evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals and the district court judgment, upholding Abu Youm's drug convictions and the denial of his motion to suppress.

title: LS Power Midcontinent, LLC v. State
description: Whether Iowa legislation granting incumbent electric transmission owners a right of first refusal for new projects is constitutional under the single-subject, title, and equal protection clauses, and whether non-incumbent competitors have standing to challenge it.
plaintiff_argument: LSP argues they have standing because the ROFR directly injures them by precluding competitive bidding, and the legislation is unconstitutional due to violations of the single-subject, title, and equal protection clauses of the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State and intervenors argue LSP lacks standing because no specific project was lost, and the ROFR legislation is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' dismissal for lack of standing, found LSP likely to succeed on the merits of its constitutional challenge, and granted a temporary injunction to stay enforcement of the ROFR, remanding the case for a decision on the merits.

title: State v. Sallis
description: Whether an officer's recollection of a motorist's barred driving status from several months prior constitutes reasonable suspicion for a traffic stop, and whether a trial court can regulate limited appearances of retained counsel in cases with appointed counsel.
plaintiff_argument: Sallis argued that the officer's information about his barred license was 'stale' and insufficient for a traffic stop, and that the denial of his retained attorney's limited appearance violated his constitutional right to counsel.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion for the stop based on prior knowledge of Sallis's barred license, and that the trial court has discretion to regulate limited appearances, especially with appointed counsel, to maintain an orderly process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sallis's conviction and sentence, ruling that the traffic stop was justified by reasonable suspicion and the denial of limited appearances was within the trial court's discretion.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds ex rel. State
description: Whether the 2020 legislation imposing a 24-hour waiting period for abortion violates the single-subject rule of the Iowa Constitution and whether issue preclusion from a prior ruling (PPH II) invalidating a 72-hour waiting period bars the State from defending the 24-hour waiting period, and if PPH II should be overruled.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that the 2020 legislation violated the single-subject rule and that issue preclusion from PPH II barred the State from relitigating the constitutionality of mandatory waiting periods. They also contended that PPH II, which recognized a fundamental right to abortion, was correctly decided and should not be overruled.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the 2020 legislation did not violate the single-subject rule, that issue preclusion did not apply, and that PPH II was wrongly decided and should be overruled, thereby removing the fundamental right to abortion under the Iowa Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's summary judgment for Planned Parenthood, concluding that the 24-hour waiting period legislation did not violate the single-subject rule and that issue preclusion did not prevent revisiting PPH II. The court overruled PPH II, holding that the Iowa Constitution does not establish a fundamental right to an abortion, and remanded the case for further proceedings to determine the appropriate constitutional standard of review.

title: Landowners v. South Central Regional Airport Agency
description: Whether the 28E Agreement, which created the South Central Regional Airport Agency (SCRAA), is unconstitutional because it binds future legislative bodies and unlawfully restricts Mahaska County's ability to terminate its delegation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The Landowners and Mahaska County argued that the 28E Agreement is unconstitutional because it binds future boards of supervisors in their legislative functions and prevents the County from exiting the agreement in the same manner it entered.
defendant_argument: The Cities of Pella and Oskaloosa argued that the 28E Agreement is valid, allows for the delegation of governmental functions, and does not unconstitutionally bind future legislative bodies.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the Cities, declaring Article XI of the 28E Agreement invalid and severing it, thereby allowing Mahaska County to withdraw from the SCRAA.

title: State v. Price-Williams
description: Whether law enforcement violated Price-Williams's Fourth Amendment and Iowa Constitution rights against unreasonable search and seizure by ordering him out of a vehicle and conducting a pat-down without reasonable suspicion, and whether his admission to possessing a firearm should be suppressed due to a lack of Miranda warning.
plaintiff_argument: Price-Williams argued that the officers lacked reasonable suspicion to justify the exit order and pat-down, and that his admission to possessing a firearm was obtained in violation of his Miranda rights.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion based on Price-Williams's prior criminal history and demeanor, justifying the exit order and pat-down, and that the pat-down was lawful regardless of the Miranda claim which the State was not relying on.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's denial of Price-Williams's motion to suppress and his conviction, finding that the officers had reasonable suspicion to order him out of the vehicle and conduct a pat-down for weapons.

title: State v. Hauge
description: Whether law enforcement acted unreasonably under the Fourth Amendment and Iowa Constitution by ordering a passenger out of a vehicle and conducting a pat-down search, and whether the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the officer's order for Hauge to exit the vehicle was necessary to facilitate a lawful arrest of another passenger, and that Hauge's consent to the pat-down was voluntary without requiring an advisement of the right to refuse.
defendant_argument: Hauge argued that law enforcement lacked justification to order him out of the vehicle and that his consent to the pat-down was not voluntary because he was not informed of his right to decline the search.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, ruling that the officer's order for the passenger to exit the vehicle was necessary for a lawful arrest and that the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.

title: State v. Basquin
description: Whether the Iowa Supreme Court's COVID-19 supervisory orders authorizing written felony guilty pleas violated precedent, due process, and separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the court's constitutional and inherent authority allowed it to permit written guilty pleas to felonies during the pandemic, and that the supervisory orders did not violate due process or the separation of powers.
defendant_argument: Basquin argued that rules of criminal procedure, precedent, and due process require an in-person plea colloquy in open court, and that the supervisory orders allowing written pleas violate due process and separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court upheld its supervisory orders as lawful exercises of its constitutional and inherent authority during the pandemic, rejected Basquin's due process and separation of powers challenges to his written plea, and affirmed his conviction.

title: State v. Lilly
description: Whether Kenneth Lee Lilly's right to an impartial jury under the United States and Iowa Constitutions was violated due to the systematic exclusion of African-Americans from jury pools.
plaintiff_argument: Lilly argued that his right to an impartial jury was violated because neither his jury nor the jury panel contained any African-Americans, and this underrepresentation was due to systematic exclusion caused by the jury selection process, specifically the source lists used.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Lilly failed to prove that the challenged practice of using voter registration, driver's license, and nonoperator identification lists caused the systematic exclusion, especially as it is a 'run-of-the-mill' practice under the Sixth Amendment, and he lacked evidence for his premises under the Iowa Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's holding that Lilly failed to prove a violation of his right to an impartial jury and affirmed his conviction.

title: State v. Wright
description: Whether a peace officer, without a warrant, can take a citizen's opaque trash bags left outside for collection, open them, and rummage through their contents for criminal investigation.
plaintiff_argument: The officer's warrantless search of his trash bags violated his constitutional rights under federal and state law, as it involved physical trespass and an invasion of his reasonable expectation of privacy, especially given local anti-scavenging ordinances.
defendant_argument: Wright abandoned his trash, thus he had no reasonable expectation of privacy in it, and the officer's conduct was justified for law enforcement purposes.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the warrantless search and seizure of Wright's trash bags violated Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and remanded the case for the suppression of evidence obtained from these searches.

title: Godfrey v. State
description: Whether Christopher J. Godfrey, an openly gay appointed state official, was subjected to sexual-orientation discrimination and retaliation under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and had his constitutional due process rights violated by Governor Branstad's actions, including a salary reduction.
plaintiff_argument: Godfrey argued that Governor Branstad's decision to request his resignation and reduce his salary was motivated by his sexual orientation, constituting discrimination and retaliation under the Iowa Civil Rights Act (ICRA). He also claimed a constitutionally protected property interest in his salary, which was violated.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued they were entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the ICRA was inapplicable (Godfrey was an officer, not an employee), there was insufficient evidence that Governor Branstad knew Godfrey was gay, Godfrey did not engage in statutorily protected activity for retaliation, and Godfrey had no constitutionally protected property interest in his salary.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the district court and remanded the matter for the entry of dismissal of the plaintiff's claims, ruling in favor of the defendants on all claims.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether the Iowa General Assembly's law, which prohibits abortion providers from participating in federally funded sex education grant programs, violates constitutional rights such as equal protection, due process, free speech, and free association.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland (PPH) argued that the Act violates its equal protection rights by unconstitutionally distinguishing between abortion providers and non-providers, and that it imposes unconstitutional conditions on the receipt of government funds by forcing PPH to give up its rights to free speech, free association, and a due process right to provide abortions.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the funding conditions are rationally related to its interest in selecting the messenger for its programs, expressing a preference for childbirth over abortion, ensuring its message is not diluted, and avoiding indirect subsidization of abortion providers. The State also contended that an abortion provider lacks a freestanding constitutional right to provide abortions, and the Act does not affect a woman's ability to obtain an abortion.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, upholding the state law that prohibits abortion providers from receiving federal grant funding for sex education programs.

title: Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement v. State
description: Whether the State of Iowa has an affirmative duty under the public trust doctrine to protect navigable waters from agricultural nonpoint source pollution, and whether the plaintiffs have standing to compel the State to enact mandatory pollution controls.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the State of Iowa violated the public trust doctrine by failing to protect the Raccoon River from agricultural pollution, leading to increased water treatment costs and impaired recreational use, and seek a mandatory remedial plan.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs lack standing because their alleged injuries are speculative and not redressable by the court, and the issue is a nonjusticiable political question that should be resolved by the legislative branch.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, concluding that the plaintiffs lacked standing and the issue was a nonjusticiable political question, and remanded with instructions to dismiss the petition.

title: State v. Sewell
description: Whether Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution guarantee a suspected drunk driver the right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding whether to take a blood alcohol test, with the plaintiff arguing for this right and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: Sewell argues that Iowa Code section 804.20 and the Iowa Constitution (Article I, sections 10 and 9) guarantee a suspected drunk driver the right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding whether to take a blood alcohol test.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Iowa Code section 804.20 does not provide a right to a private phone consultation, and the Iowa Constitution's right to counsel only attaches in criminal prosecutions, which do not commence before the decision to take a chemical test, thus no due process violation occurred.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction and sentence, holding that Sewell was not entitled to a private phone consultation with counsel under either Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution, and his motion to suppress was properly denied.

title: State v. Treptow
description: Whether Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7, which limit direct appeals for guilty pleas and mandate postconviction relief for ineffective assistance of counsel claims, violate the separation of powers, equal protection, and due process doctrines, and whether the defendant has established good cause to pursue a direct appeal.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7 are constitutional, do not violate separation of powers, equal protection, or due process, and that Treptow failed to establish good cause for a direct appeal.
defendant_argument: Treptow argued that Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7 violate separation of powers, equal protection, and due process, and that he had good cause to appeal, especially regarding the factual basis of his guilty plea.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Treptow's appeal, ruling that he failed to establish good cause for a direct appeal and upholding the constitutionality of Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7.

title: Hrbek v. State
description: Whether Iowa Code section 822.3A, which prohibits represented postconviction-relief applicants from filing pro se supplemental documents, is applicable retrospectively and constitutional, or if it violates the separation of powers doctrine and an applicant's right to file such documents.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, John Hrbek, argued that the new law should not be applied retrospectively to his pending case and that it is unconstitutional, violating the separation of powers doctrine and his constitutional right to file pro se supplemental documents.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Iowa, argued that the new law applies prospectively to all filings after its effective date, is constitutional, and does not violate the separation of powers or any constitutional right to hybrid representation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, ruling that Iowa Code section 822.3A applies to Hrbek's case and is constitutional, rejecting his claims that it violates the separation of powers or any constitutional right to file pro se supplemental documents.

title: State ex rel. Dickey v. Besler
description: Whether a citizen has standing to bring a quo warranto action challenging the timeliness of a judicial appointment when the appointing authorities (Governor and Chief Justice) have both accepted the appointment as timely, and whether such a challenge is justiciable.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor failed to make a timely appointment, so Besler unlawfully holds office, and Dickey has standing as a citizen to challenge it, making the issue justiciable.
defendant_argument: Dickey lacks standing, the Governor's appointment was timely, and the court should not intervene due to principles of comity and separation of powers, rendering the issue nonjusticiable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, concluding that the case presents a nonjusticiable controversy because both the Governor and the Chief Justice deferred to and accepted the view that the appointment was timely.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether Iowa Code section 814.6A, which prohibits represented defendants from filing pro se documents, violates the separation of powers doctrine, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is a proper exercise of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: Thompson argued that Iowa Code section 814.6A is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers doctrine and impairs the essential functioning of appellate courts by denying a defendant's right to present legal claims.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code section 814.6A is a proper exercise of the legislative department's constitutional authority to regulate practice and procedure in Iowa's courts and does not violate the separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Thompson's convictions for attempting to obtain a prescription drug by deceit and rejected his constitutional challenge to Iowa Code section 814.6A, upholding the law.
